title: How long? (Psalm 13)
hook: injustice cries out, and God hears the cry

segments.voice: Yesterday, when a child dies: a mother in Ramah who would not be comforted, and hope spoken beside her tears. Your line was rachel weeping. Did you hold one grieving parent in your heart? Day one thousand four hundred four.

Two words, and a question mark. They are on protest signs and in hospital waiting rooms. A tenant says them about the landlord who won't fix the heat. A family says them about a trial that keeps getting postponed. A child says them in the back seat, and a whole people says them across generations. How long? It sounds like impatience. In the Bible it is something else: a prayer, and a cry about what is wrong. A short psalm asks it again and again, and the Bible keeps answering that the cry is heard. Today: how long?

Not long ago, this psalm's first line came up as an argument with God. Today, listen for the next verse, where a third figure enters, the enemy: "How long shall I take counsel in my soul, having sorrow in my heart daily? how long shall mine enemy be exalted over me?" Someone is winning who shouldn't be. That's what turns how long from a sigh into a cry about injustice. And the Bible says that kind of cry is heard. In Exodus, God speaks from the burning bush: "I have surely seen the affliction of my people which are in Egypt, and have heard their cry by reason of their taskmasters; for I know their sorrows." Seen, heard, known, and every one of those words points at people being worked by taskmasters. The prophet Habakkuk opens his book with the same complaint, about violence and judgment gone crooked: "O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!" And at the far end of the Bible, in Revelation, the souls of those slain for the word of God cry out from under the altar: "How long, O Lord, holy and true?" From the psalms to the last book, the question is never thrown out. Then Psalm thirteen ends in a strange place. Nothing outside has changed yet. The enemy is still there. But the voice says, "But I have trusted in thy mercy; my heart shall rejoice in thy salvation." The cry and the trust come from the same mouth, in the same short psalm. In the Bible, how long is one of the ways people pray about what's wrong, and keep praying.
screen: `HOW LONG, O LORD, HOLY AND TRUE?`
`BUT I HAVE TRUSTED IN THY MERCY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: add your voice for justice. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one wrong that has gone on too long. It might be far away, or it might be on your own street: someone underpaid, someone unheard, someone waiting for a hearing that never comes. Name it to yourself plainly. If you pray, you can bring it to God in the psalm's own words: how long, O Lord? If you don't, just hold it in the open. Then choose one small way to add your voice after the bell: a call, a letter, a signature, a conversation, showing up. The bell holds the time.
How long? The cry of Psalm thirteen, spoken straight to God when wrong is winning, and kept in scripture as a prayer.
Your line: how long, o lord? Today, when you see something unjust, don't swallow the question. Say it, to God or out loud, and then do the one thing you chose. Day one thousand four hundred four.

howItsDone: Christians pray the lament psalms, including Psalm 13, in worship and in private, and churches and Christian groups bring that cry into action through advocacy, legal aid, protest and care for people who are being wronged.

fork.setup: you're the voice of Psalm 13. God seems to have forgotten you, and your enemy is winning. what do you do?
options: stay silent, because questioning God is not allowed.
ask God straight out, how long?, and then speak your trust.
give up on God and stop praying.
fork.reveal: the psalm does both: it asks how long again and again, then says, but I have trusted in thy mercy. the question and the trust share one short psalm.

original.note: Hebrew: until where? how long? — the words that open the cries of Psalm 13.

trapdoor: what you thought: asking God how long is impatience, or a lack of faith.
what it means: Psalm 13 asks it straight to God's face, and the Bible keeps the question as a prayer.
what a scholar hears: a lament psalm: complaint, then a plea, then trust. the turn to trust comes before anything outside has changed.
